title: Branch-Price-and-Cut
contribution: Textbook synthesis (closing chapter of Branch-and-Price) of how a root-node Dantzig-Wolfe column generation becomes an exact branch-price-and-cut method: integrality testing, cuts and branching stated in x or λ and placed in master or pricing domain, judged by their effect on pricing, plus MIP-solver practices and implementation advice, with small new items (clique cuts on master variables for set partitioning, the floor form (7.65), z-cuts in the pricing domain) (pp. 1, 94-95).
problem_entry: Only the root LP of a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation is solved so far; a fractional solution must be cut or branched, raising what 'integer' means for a master solution, where a decision goes, and what it does to pricing; GENCOL experience: difficulties came from branching and cutting rules (pp. 1, 3-10, 22-24, 94).
key_idea: Every cut and branching decision is a constraint in x or λ placed in master group A (robust, only dual terms in pricing) or pricing domain D (convexified, stronger, may change pricing); the deciding distinction is whether master coefficients are linear in x; branch on sums of λ over columns satisfying a pricing-checkable condition on x, never on a single λ; 'how you branch determines how you decompose(d)' (pp. 8-10, 17-18, 22-24, 29-38, 45-49).
assumptions: Pure ILP min c⊺x, Ax ≥ b, Dx ≥ d, x integer, feasible with finite optimum; MIP case only sketched (pp. 4, 50); D a polytope or polyhedral cone, one pricing problem adaptable to blocks (p. 29); relies on Hilbert-Giles-Pulleyblank, at most m positive λ, no identical columns, integer data where rounded; rank-1 integer master cuts (pp. 13-19, 25, 37, 39, 88); hand-sized instances and published applications, no MIPLIB (pp. 14, 46, 68, 79-93).
proof_devices: Proposition 7.1 (Vanderbeck 2000): separating a fractional column from the convex hull of the others by an integer hyperplane (pp. 30-31)
Proposition 7.2: halving the fractionality by splitting at the midpoint of a differing coordinate, fewer than log m bounds for a basic solution (pp. 35-37)
Ryan-Foster existence from a row covered by two fractional columns plus a separating row (pp. 38-39)
ceiling linearization y ≤ x + 1 − ε, y integer, for Chvátal-Gomory master cuts in pricing (pp. 19-20)
coefficient g_x computed in pricing by inequalities (7.63) or one inequality per branch using the branching dual sign (7.66) (pp. 31-35)
disaggregation by a zero-cost balanced transportation problem (pp. 5-6, 28)
reduced-cost arc fixing via forward/backward labeling (7.96) (pp. 51-52)
counter-example: clique cuts satisfied by every independent-set column (pp. 11-12)
experiments: No own study; hand-computed toy runs (VRPTW one cut closing 94.1% of gap, z-cuts solving the TCSPP, five-node tree; pp. 14-17, 68-72) and quoted literature results (RC101.25 2-path cuts, Air Canada 5.7 h, CN locomotive 1.1% saving at 33% more CPU; pp. 80, 89, 93); no MIPLIB, baselines, seeds; several defaults without data (pp. 53, 55-56).
positioning: Branching half a synthesis of Vanderbeck's œuvre (pp. 28, 95); historical credit to Ryan-Foster and Desrosiers et al. 1984 (pp. 94-95); direct critique of misreadings (inter-task not a Ryan-Foster case p. 40, no-branching 'column generation approaches' p. 64, most-fractional rejected p. 44); MIP-solver literature as reference for the tree, SCIP recommended, GCG described (pp. 23, 44, 59, 63, 67); own group cited sparingly (pp. 12, 61-63, 94, 96).
writing: Teaching register in first person plural with direct address, epigraphs, fourteen titled Notes carrying warnings, Examples opening with one-line lessons, two running toy instances, humour and foreign-language asides, hedged advice vs unhedged propositions, sections ending in takeaways (pp. 1, 4, 9-16, 22, 49, 64-65, 76, 83).
limits_future: Prop. 7.1 non-constructive (p. 33); odd-circuit cuts no integrality guarantee, no efficient k-path separation (pp. 78-79, 83); relaxed pricing can enlarge the tree (p. 57); MIP branching only sketched (p. 50); implementations may be fruitless (p. 67); future directions left as Exercise 7.21, the only one without solution (p. 100).

method_links.note: Implementation guide is Method 1 in the authors' order: paper first, compact MILP with real data as pipeline and benchmark, Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation kept simple, framework (SCIP) and GCG probe, acceleration only after the basic code runs, read through three indicators; the investment may be fruitless.

Step 6: original variables are not always the branching object with aggregated identical blocks (branch on λ-sums or auxiliary variables); stop rule softer: MILP pricing used where no combinatorial algorithm exists.

Claims sized to evidence: 94.1% cut 'not always so effective' with the reason; price-and-branch not called branch-and-price; CPU cost reported next to savings; shortcut backed only as far as results go.
Evaluation advice diagnostic on one representative set, not the two-set protocol; numerical defaults carry no counts; quoted results from 1997-1999 and not re-run; 2021 paper cited as technique only.
The chapter is Method 4's product: literature rewritten in one notation (two spaces times two placements), yielding small new results and named corrections, with open items published.
Small instances computed completely, but to explain, not to map an option space; branching option space written down but the choice left to research and experimentation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: pricing-compatibility filter for cuts and branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: cuts and branching judged by whether pricing survives them
decisions in original variables alone cannot be stronger than those using extra variables

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: escalate cut strength only while pricing can bear it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: lift weak robust cuts to strong non-robust ones only if still violated; roll back cuts when pricing gets too hard

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry the MIP solver's toolkit into branch-and-price
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: candidate ranking, preprocessing and primal heuristics carried over from MIP solvers

transferable: Before implementing a cut family, check it against the columns. If every column (e.g., every independent set) already satisfies it, the reformulated cut can never be violated (vertex-coloring clique cuts, pp. 11–12).

Add cheap a priori cuts: the objective-rounding cut c⊺x ≥ ⌈z_MP⌉ for integer costs, and the rounded capacity cut for S = C (pp. 13, 15). With integer costs, impose LB ≤ c⊺x ≤ UB inside pricing to delete non-optimal columns (pp. 15–17, 88).

Design master-variable branching as "the sum of λ over the columns that satisfy a condition on x" (a cost interval, a customer count, a bound on one x_j). Compute the 0/1 coefficient in pricing with one inequality per branch, using the sign of the branching dual ((7.66), p. 32; g_x = x_j in the binary case, p. 35).

With a labeling pricing, prefer inter-task (follow-on) branching to Ryan-Foster and track only the last covered task in the label (pp. 40–41; Exercise 7.10, pp. 97–98). With a graph pricing, implement same/differ as node contraction and edge insertion (p. 75).

Never delete columns in the tree; fix them by local bounds that a node applies when it is processed (p. 26). With an explicit master inside a MILP solver, copy its local x-bounds into pricing yourself (p. 24).

Diagnose before accelerating: run the basic code on relatively large instances and read column generation iterations, RMP against pricing time, and node count. Then pick from the technique family for the dominant bottleneck (pp. 52–59).

Starting defaults, to be measured: remove m columns when the RMP holds 3m, with at least 5 iterations between removals (p. 55). In multi-block pricing, stop after 3 successful pricing problems, or after 2 failures and at least 1 success, and price fully at the end (p. 56).

Separate the weak robust version of a cut with existing heuristics, and lift it to the strong non-robust version only if it stays violated after re-optimization (Note 7.14, p. 83). Roll back the last round of cuts and branch instead when pricing exceeds a label-count threshold (p. 57).
Run strong branching in two phases: re-optimize only the RMP for every candidate, then run column and cut generation with heuristic pricing for a shortlist (p. 58).

Run the MIP solver's own heuristics on the compact model to seed the RMP. Dive on λ only when it is close to 1, and otherwise fix arcs. Finish by solving the RMP of all generated columns as a MILP (diving with sub-MILP) (pp. 61–63).
When the RMP starts from big-M artificials, check M against the reduced cost the first feasible column needs before pruning a node as infeasible (p. 70).
Branch first to make a low-dimensional substructure explicit, then cut with its facets on that branch (at most two locomotive types per train, pp. 91–92).
Call a code without a branching rule a restricted-master heuristic (price-and-branch), not branch-and-price (pp. 60, 64).
coauthors: J. Desrosiers, G. Desaulniers, J.B. Gauthier

quotes.text: experimentation tells us that in general “most fractional” is the worst one can do: this rule is no better than random branching and should be avoided (Achterberg et al., 2005).
We should not hide that even a large investment in an implementation may turn out to be fruitless in the end.
